ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all proposed directors, officers, shareholders, and any person holding 25% or greater beneficial interest against: (i) the FINTRAC Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) list and Domestic PEP regime under the PCMLTFA; (ii) the OFAC SDN List, applicable because the customs brokerage's USD Automated_Broker_Interface_ACH and wire rails touch the U.S. financial system; (iii) the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List; (iv) the Global Affairs Canada consolidated sanctions list under the Special Economic Measures Act, the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, and the United Nations Act; and (v) Canadian domestic criminal and civil forfeiture databases. Enhanced Due Diligence is mandatory for PEPs, non-resident UBOs, high-risk jurisdictions, and entities presenting nominee instruments. FINTRAC requires a written AML/ATF program, risk assessment, ongoing transaction monitoring of ACH/wire payment rails, and a five-year record retention period. Any positive sanctions hit imposes immediate refusal of incorporation, Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) filing, and disclosure to FINTRAC within 30 days.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (CORES) via corporateonline.alberta.ca; Federal NUANS search via Corporations Canada (iservice canada.ca) for cross-provincial or federal name clearance
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must be expressed in English or French using the 26-letter Latin alphabet, Arabic numerals, and standard punctuation; a distinctive element may contain a foreign-language word only if accompanied by a statutory English or French descriptive element; non-Latin scripts, diacritical transliterations, and alternative character sets are not accepted on Alberta registry records; the name must be distinguishable from all existing corporate, trade name, and registered trademark records as confirmed by a NUANS report; the legal element must be one of the prescribed Alberta ULC designations, namely 'Unlimited Liability Company', 'Unlimited Liability Corporation', or the abbreviation 'ULC' or 'U.L.C.'
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon rejection by the Alberta Corporate Registry, the applicant or its legal counsel may: (1) submit a revised name request in CORES by replacing the conflicting distinctive element or removing the offending token while preserving the statutory ULC element; (2) where rejection arises from a sensitive or prohibited token, file a written reconsideration request to the Registrar under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta) along with supporting statutory declarations, the proposed business plan evidencing lawful use for customs brokerage, and written consent letters from any competent regulatory body whose terminology is implicated, including the Canada Border Services Agency for 'Customs Broker'; (3) where a NUANS conflict is alleged, file, within 14 days of the notice, a formal submission with evidence of prior common-law use in Alberta and proof of the applicant's distinctiveness; (4) if refusal is maintained, lodge an administrative appeal to the internal Appeals Commission for Corporate Registry Decisions, with a subsequent judicial review application to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta; (5) concurrently reserve a fallback name in CORES to prevent delay of incorporation, fulfilling the 90-day reservation window by effecting incorporation before expiration. Where a federal NUANS name is required due to cross-provincial customs operations, the same appeal path applies mutatis mutandis through Corporations Canada, culminating in judicial review in the Federal Court.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Conditional. The Alberta Business Corporations Act requires a registered office in Alberta that is a physical address capable of receiving service of process during normal business hours and where the corporate records and minute book are maintained. A pure virtual mailbox is not permissible. Because the entity is a Licensed Customs Brokerage House, the Canada Border Services Agency and FINTRAC mandate a genuine Canadian business location where customs records, client files, broker working papers, and AML/ATF documents are physically or securely accessible for inspection. A virtual office is therefore acceptable only when paired with a compliant physical operational address, a resident CBSA-licensed customs broker, and a substantive commercial presence in Alberta.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry via authorized online service provider
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS pre-screening or Alberta name search; submit a name reservation for at least 90 days for the exact proposed ULC legal name ending with 'Unlimited Liability Corporation' or 'ULC'.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If name is refused, amend the request with a new NUANS report and pay a new reservation fee; file a consent from the holder of a trademark if the refusal is based on confusingly similar marks.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Draft and File Articles of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete Form AB-INC-01 for an unlimited liability corporation; specify capital structure, classes of shares, and restrictions; state the registered office address and first directors; include the ULC designation required under Alberta law.
required_dossiers: Notice of address of registered office
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a query or rejection, correct the defect in the articles, resubmit within 30 days, and pay any additional filing fee; request a formal Registrar's opinion if the rejection is procedural.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Pay Filing Fees and Obtain Certificate of Incorporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the filing fee (approx. CAD 275 online) and all statutory documents; upon approval, receive the Certificate of Incorporation which is conclusive evidence of corporate existence.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If certificate is lost or delayed, request a certified copy by declaration; if incorporation is voided, apply for revival under s. 209 ABCA within prescribed period.

step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold first board meeting or furnish unanimous consent resolution; adopt bylaws regulating share transfers, meetings, officers, and corporate powers; appoint the initial directors and officers; open a corporate bank account under the ULC name.
required_dossiers: Written consent to act as director
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a director declines consent, appoint a substitute director immediately and file an amended initial notice within 15 days; cure any deficiency by unanimous consent resolution.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: File Federal and Provincial Business Registry Notices
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Alberta Provincial Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register for a federal Business Number (BN) and GST/HST account; register with the Alberta Corporate Registry as a provincial extra-provincial equivalent if none; obtain an Alberta Tax Identification Number for employer and corporate tax purposes.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA registration is delayed, file a paper Form RC1 and provide additional service office screening; appeal any incorrectly assigned tax status through the CRA objections process.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Register as Customs Broker with CBSA
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) - Trade Programs and Licensing Directorate
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit CBSA Form B2 for customs broker licence application; provide corporate details, the name of at least one qualified individual broker, proof of bond or security, and evidence of ULC legitimacy; pass suitability review and pay the licence fee.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation and ULC registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If licence is refused or suspended, file a written representation to CBSA and request a review tribunal hearing under the Customs Act; submit a corrective action plan if deficiencies relate to compliance systems.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Federal tax administration; provincial counterpart for Alberta: Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration). CRA online portal: My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/digital-services-individuals/account-registration-access.html). Alberta corporate registry: Corporate Registry, Service Alberta.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity establishing a Canadian Unlimited Liability Corporation (ULC) in Alberta must first complete provincial incorporation through Service Alberta Corporate Registry, obtaining an Alberta corporation number. Concurrently, the entity must apply to the CRA for a Business Number (BN/RT account) via the CRA's 'Register Business Account' online service or by completing Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number and Certain Program Accounts). The BN must be obtained before filing corporate income tax (T2) and GST/HST returns. If the ULC is resident in Alberta or has Canadian source business income, it must also register for the Alberta Corporate Tax Act account (Alberta corporate income tax) and, if applicable, the Alberta provincial employer accounts. For customs brokerage activities, separate CRA customs account identifiers are obtained through the CBSA Customs Self-Assessment or the RCA program, but the BN remains the master identifier. Proof of Canadian address and an authorised Canadian representative may be required for non-resident directors or management.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation (for Canadian tax purposes, an Alberta ULC is generally treated as a corporation subject to the Income Tax Act; however, under the Canada–U.S. Income Tax Convention Article IV(7), a ULC resident in Canada may be disregarded as a fiscally transparent entity if all of its owners are residents of the United States, enabling look-through treatment for U.S.-parented groups). For Alberta provincial purposes, the ULC is taxable as a corporation. Territorial scope: federal and Alberta provincial corporate income tax apply on worldwide income of a Canadian-resident corporation, with foreign tax credit relief.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No formal Canadian 'check-the-box' election exists; entity classification is determined by de facto corporate status under the Canada Business Corporations Act or provincial legislation. Under the Canada–U.S. Tax Treaty, a ULC may be treated as a disregarded entity for U.S. federal tax purposes if all U.S.-resident owners file Form 8832 with the IRS; for Canadian tax purposes, the entity remains taxable unless the specific treaty tie-breaker rules apply. Hybrid mismatch rules under section 18.4 and 18.6 of the Income Tax Act may restrict deductions for payments made by entities subject to hybrid mismatch arrangements, especially where a ULC is fiscally transparent in the United States but opaque in Canada.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax), and Alberta provincial Retail Sales Tax is not applicable (Alberta is a GST-only province with no provincial sales tax)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 (worldwide taxable supplies, including zero-rated supplies, measured over a single calendar quarter or consecutively over four calendar quarters). A customs brokerage house providing services to non-residents may be required to register if the threshold is exceeded; voluntary registration is permitted. If exceeding CAD 30,000 in the previous four calendar quarters or currently exceeding the small supplier limit, mandatory GST registration applies. A non-resident carrying on business in Canada is also required to register if not a 'small supplier' and if making taxable supplies in Canada.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: There is currently no mandatory real-time fiscal clearance or digital stamping regime for GST/HST sales invoices in Canada. However, CRA imposes electronic record-keeping requirements for GST/HST registrants, requiring that accounts and records be kept at the place of business or residence in Canada and be made available for inspection. The CBSA uses the Automated Customs Document System (ACDS) and the National Customs Ruling (NCR) program; customs brokers must file electronic export/import declarations via the Canadian Customs Automated Data Exchange (CADEX), the Automated Broker Interface (ABI), or the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) portal. For GST/HST on commercial goods, the CBSA's customs invoice may be transmitted via the Customs Commercial System (CCS). Electronic data interchange is mandatory for customs brokers licensed by the CBSA; there is no tax-specific clearance stamp, but PEPPITO reporting and eManifest are required for electronic trade data.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating applies to exports of goods that are shipped directly from Canada to a destination outside Canada by the vendor or an agent, where the goods are not further processed or incorporated into other goods in Canada. For services, zero-rating applies to services rendered to a non-resident if the services are performed entirely outside Canada, or if the services are in respect of tangible personal property located outside Canada, or if the service is a 'global supply' under Section 23 of Part V of Schedule IX to the Excise Tax Act. A customs brokerage house may zero-rate its services to a non-resident where the benefit of the service is supplied outside Canada and the service is supplied for consumption outside Canada. However, customs brokerage services relating to imported goods may be taxable at 5% GST if the supply is made in Canada and not an exported service. Export zero-rating claims require proof of export/offshore service delivery, including contracts, shipping documents, freight forwarder evidence, or foreign customs entry records. A GST registered exporter must retain documentation demonstrating that tangible property was exported within a reasonable period (usually 60 days of the billing date, but subject to CRA administrative policy).
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CBSA Form B13A / ACI eManifest cargo data)
Bill of Lading / Airway Bill (original or electronic)
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank payment confirmation evidencing receipt of foreign currency proceeds
Proof of insurance and freight / freight forwarder's certificate
Export permit or licence where the goods are controlled (e.g., ECCL, CUSMA certificate if applicable)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA and CBSA conduct rigorous audit programs for zero-rated exports. If an exporter fails to substantiate export within a reasonable time, the GST/HST assessed tax is recoverable with interest (5% risk-free rate plus penalties). Under the Excise Tax Act, false statements or misrepresentations in a return can result in a penalty equal to 25% of the tax (greater of 50% of the understated tax or CAD 100), plus fines of up to CAD 25,000 for summary conviction and CAD 100,000 for indictable offence. Section 23 of the Excise Tax Act and the General Anti-Avoidance Rule are used to deny refunds/remission claims where a scheme involves artificial transactions. For customs brokerage, the CBSA may impose administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) of up to CAD 25,000 per violation under the Customs Act, plus revocation of the broker licence for repeated failures to substantiate exports. Retrospective clawbacks are permitted through a reassessment period of four years (or more in cases of misrepresentation or fraud).

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) established under the Bank of Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. B-2) as the central monetary authority. Foreign-exchange and prudential supervision of deposit-taking institutions is exercised by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) under the Bank Act; anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing oversight is exercised by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act; customs duty and GST collection on importations is administered by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) under the Customs Act. Canada maintains no dedicated exchange-control ministry or foreign-exchange licensing body following the revocation of the wartime Exchange Control Orders in 1951.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Full de jure and de facto convertibility for both current-account and capital-account transactions consistent with IMF Article VIII obligations. The Canadian dollar floats freely; no Bank of Canada approval is required for dividend remittances, capital repatriation, interest, royalties, management fees, or customs-brokerage service payments to or from non-residents. Material constraints are limited to: (i) Part XIII non-resident withholding tax at the 25% statutory rate, treaty-reduced (e.g., 5% portfolio / 15% direct dividends under the Canada-United States Tax Convention), on payments by the Alberta ULC to its foreign member; (ii) FINTRAC reporting thresholds of CAD 10,000 for cross-border electronic funds transfers and large cash transactions; (iii) sanctions compliance under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Freezing Assets of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act; and (iv) Investment Canada Act notification thresholds for acquisition of control of a Canadian business. The ULC pass-through eligibility under US check-the-box rules has no Canadian exchange-control consequence, but triggers Part XIV branch tax filings if the ULC is deemed to carry on a Canadian business for the benefit of a non-resident member. Profit remittance and capital flight controls are absent; restrictions apply only through tax, AML, and sanctions channels.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: No statutory surrender obligation exists. Canada has not imposed export-proceeds surrender, a mandatory conversion timeline, or a required conversion ratio since 1951. Export and brokerage service receipts may be retained offshore in any freely usable currency, converted at market rates, or applied directly to foreign supplier payments. Practical compliance requirements are limited to: (i) retention of commercial evidence (customs broker invoices, B3 declarations, bills of lading, Cargo Control Documents) for source-of-funds verification; (ii) FINTRAC electronic funds transfer reporting for any cross-border transfer of CAD 10,000 or more; and (iii) Canada Revenue Agency / Statistics Canada balance-of-payments coding for the export of customs-brokerage services. CBSA imposes no foreign-exchange conversion conditions on brokerage fees.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Rating: Medium as supplementary corridor; Low as primary treasury rail. Foreign digital EMI/neobank platforms (Wise, Airwallex, Payoneer, Ebury, Currencycloud) are not authorized banks under the Bank Act and may not accept deposits in Canada unless licensed as a Schedule III authorised foreign bank or operating through a registered Canadian payment service provider under the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA), whose registration regime is administered by the Bank of Canada and is being phased in from 2024. For a licensed customs broker, EMI rails cannot support CBSA duty and tax remittances, CADEX/ACH clearing, customs bond lodgement, or the no. 1 Customs Revenue Account; those functions require a Canadian-chartered bank account. EMIs are acceptable only for low-value disbursements to foreign sub-agents and small foreign suppliers, provided the platform is RPAA-registered or partnered with a Schedule I bank, and the broker maintains full trust-account separation of client duty funds. Commingling client customs-dedicated funds in an offshore EMI is inconsistent with CBSA broker compliance expectations and would constitute an AML red flag.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No federal statute mandates in-person appearance. Under the PCMLTFA and FINTRAC guidance, identity may be verified by the two-document method, the credit-file method, the affidavit method, or the credible-reference method, with remote video verification recognised. In practice, the Big Six banks require at least one Canadian-resident director or authorised signatory to complete either an in-branch interview or an enhanced video interview with notarised or apostilled identification; non-resident members of the Alberta ULC may be onboarded remotely using a certified passport, proof of address, and a legal opinion. Mandated documentation for an Alberta ULC: certificate of incorporation or continuance under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta); current register of members with full beneficial-ownership disclosure; by-laws and unanimous member agreement; board or member resolution authorising account opening and naming signatories; and an Alberta legal opinion confirming the unlimited liability of members, the validity of corporate authority, and the absence of bearer or nominee shares.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Pass-through eligible ULC with non-resident (typically US) member ownership is flagged as a potential shell or tax-motivated vehicle with opaque beneficial ownership and unlimited liability structure.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified Alberta certificate of incorporation or continuance; current register of members with complete name, address, date of birth, citizenship, and proportion of ownership; unanimous member agreement; certified by-laws; Alberta legal opinion addressing unlimited liability and signatory authority; IRS Form 8832 check-the-box election where applicable; CRS/FATCA self-certifications (Form W-8BEN-E for the foreign member and Form W-9 for any US individual); CRA business number and tax account clearances; evidence of Canadian substance including office lease, employee payroll records, Alberta business licence, and the CBSA customs broker licence.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Customs brokerage involves handling third-party importer funds for duties, GST, and penalties, creating deposit-taking-like exposure and potential money-laundering through duty evasion or trade-based money laundering.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Valid CBSA customs broker licence and AMPS (Administrative Monetary Penalty System) compliance history; executed client service agreements and powers of attorney for customs transactions; policies demonstrating segregation of client-held duty and tax funds in a dedicated Canadian-chartered trust or clearing account with monthly bank reconciliation; customs security bond with a licensed Canadian surety; internal AML/CTF program, sanctions screening logs, and transaction monitoring procedures; CRA GST/HST and income tax registration confirmations; audited or reviewed financial statements confirming no unregulated deposit-taking.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-frequency cross-border EFTs and payments to foreign shipping, logistics, and overseas counterparties in FATF grey-list or sanctions-restricted corridors trigger enhanced due diligence and EFTR/STR reporting thresholds.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Comprehensive transaction ledger with full commercial documentation for each settlement (B3 customs declarations, commercial invoices, bills of lading, air waybills, Cargo Control Documents); executed corporate compliance attestation confirming no dealings with sanctioned entities; PEP and sanctions screening results with escalation logs; source-of-wealth declaration and bank reference from the foreign member; FINTRAC EFTR and STR filing calendar showing timely reporting; independent audit comfort letter validating the trade-flow trail.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unlimited liability of members may create uncertainty for the bank's credit exposure and may trigger separate CDD on each member if a member is a natural person subject to personal insolvency risk.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Unconditional and irrevocable parent or member guarantee supported by the guarantor's audited financial statements; ULC asset schedule and insurance certificates including errors-and-omissions and cyber liability policies; subordination and contribution agreements among members; solvency certificate issued by the ULC CFO under board resolution; Alberta legal opinion explaining the liability cascade and the enforceability of unlimited liability against each member; confirmation that no member is subject to insolvency proceedings.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Capital contributions from the foreign parent or non-resident member to the Alberta ULC must be routed as an inward direct investment under Statistics Canada's Balance of Payments classification (equity capital credit, code 0810 / liability 500). Use SWIFT MT103 or Fedwire referencing the ULC's Canadian Standard Settlement Instructions: 5-digit branch transit plus 3-digit institution number plus account number (Canada does not use IBAN), with the receiving bank's SWIFT BIC. Payment narrative must include the ULC legal name, its CBSA customs broker licence number, and the phrase 'Capital contribution / subscription to unlimited liability corporation'. FATCA/CRS documentation (Form W-8BEN-E for a US corporate member, Form W-9 for US individuals) must be on file before crediting. No exchange-control approval is required; however, the receiving bank must file a FINTRAC EFTR for any aggregated cross-border transfer of CAD 10,000 or more. Funds should first be landed in the Capital Escrow Account and then converted to CAD at a pre-agreed bank spot or forward rate. Crypto, third-party nominee accounts, and personal accounts are prohibited routing channels and constitute immediate KYC rejection triggers.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Rails available to the customs broker: (1) CBSA duty and tax remittances through the Customs Commercial System / Customs Self-Assessment using the broker's no. 1 Customs Revenue Account, or via Automated Clearing (ACH debit) under the federal Single Window Initiative, or by direct wire referencing the importer's B3 declaration and customs office code; (2) GST on importations paid to the GST Customs Account via the CBSA 'GST/Tax Account' levy codes; (3) supplier and freight payments using SWIFT MT103 with full beneficiary details and IMF BPM6 / Statistics Canada service-payment purpose codes ('customs brokerage and logistics services'); (4) commercial documentary letters of credit and standby letters of credit under UCP600 for large bonded-transit management projects; (5) settlement payments to the customs surety bond issuer; and (6) intercompany dividend or management-fee remittances to the foreign member subject to Part XIII withholding via SWIFT MT103 with the applicable treaty rate code. Every outbound payment must preserve the underlying customs declaration audit trail; client duty monies must be remitted from the segregated clearing account and never commingled with operating funds. FINTRAC EFTR must be filed for each cross-border transfer of CAD 10,000 or more, and sanctions screening must be pre-payment.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards (CAD against USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, and CNY) with tenors up to 12 months, documented under a Canadian Master Agreement or ISDA/CSA, available from Schedule I authorised banks
Cross-currency swaps (fixed-against-fixed and floating-against-floating) for hedging long-term parent funding, duty-asset mismatches, and intercompany loan exposures
FX swaps for short-term liquidity management of CAD settlement balances and customs bond collateral
Purchased European-style vanilla FX options on major pairs (writing unhedged options is generally not permitted without bank approval)

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) exclusively for non-convertible or restricted Asian currencies (offshore CNH, INR, KRW, VND, NGN) transacted with licensed banks; retail OTC binary or structured products are prohibited

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Combined federal (15%) + Alberta provincial (8%) = 23% general corporate rate; federal small business rate 9% (on first CA$500,000 active business income), Alberta small business rate 2% => 11% combined for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs). An Alberta ULC owned by a non-resident is not a CCPC and therefore ranks ineligible for the small business deduction.
